title: High-Dose Intranasal Naloxone & Nalmefene
keywords: Kloxxado is FDA-approved 8mg intranasal naloxone, twice the standard Narcan 4mg dose
Opvee is FDA-approved 2.7mg intranasal nalmefene, longer half-life than naloxone
neither has shown a proven survival benefit over standard-dose naloxone
both carry a real risk of more severe and more protracted precipitated withdrawal
standard-dose naloxone with retitration and an infusion for recurrence remains the evidence-based default
sources: FDA approval: Opvee (nalmefene 2.7mg intranasal), for ages ≥ 12.

Efficacy/safety comparison to standard-dose naloxone — no proven survival benefit, increased withdrawal severity — WebSearch-verified before writing, consistent with this app's existing tox-opioids reference's standard-dose-first philosophy.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-14, Batch 5), the specific FDA-approved high-dose/long-acting products the audit flagged, framed with the actual evidence (which does not support routine preference for these over standard-dose naloxone) rather than the marketing rationale alone. Cross-linked with, and deliberately consistent with, the existing tox-opioids reference's standard-naloxone-first, retitrate-and-infuse philosophy — this card supplements that guidance with the specific product details, it doesn't contradict it.

mechanism: Competitive opioid receptor antagonism, same mechanism as standard-dose naloxone (Kloxxado is simply a higher-concentration naloxone nasal spray) — nalmefene (Opvee) is a different molecule with a substantially longer half-life than naloxone, marketed specifically to outlast long-acting/high-potency synthetic opioids like fentanyl and its analogs without needing re-dosing as often.
onset: Comparable to standard intranasal naloxone — within a few minutes.
duration: Naloxone (any dose): roughly 30-90 minutes, generally shorter than the opioid being reversed, especially fentanyl analogs and methadone — hence the standard teaching to observe for re-sedation regardless of which naloxone product/dose is used. Nalmefene: meaningfully longer-acting than naloxone, which is the specific rationale for its development, though this same long duration is also what prolongs precipitated withdrawal if it occurs.
dosing:
Kloxxado (naloxone 8mg intranasal spray): one spray (8mg) into one nostril; may repeat every 2-3 minutes with additional doses in alternating nostrils if needed, per product labeling — this is DOUBLE the standard Narcan 4mg intranasal dose.
Opvee (nalmefene 2.7mg intranasal spray): one spray (2.7mg) into one nostril; may repeat every 2-3 minutes in alternating nostrils if inadequate response, per product labeling. Approved for ages 12 and older.
Both: the SAME general principles as standard-dose naloxone apply — titrate to adequate spontaneous respiration, not full arousal, and observe for a period appropriate to the suspected opioid's duration (see tox-opioids).
cautions: Precautions: NEITHER product has demonstrated a proven survival benefit over standard-dose (4mg intranasal or 0.4mg IV/IM) naloxone in the available evidence to date — the fentanyl-era marketing rationale (standard doses being 'not enough' for high-potency synthetic opioids) has not translated into demonstrated outcome improvement in real-world data.

AEs: both are associated with MORE SEVERE and MORE PROTRACTED precipitated opioid withdrawal compared to standard-dose naloxone — for a patient who is opioid-dependent, over-reversal produces genuine suffering (vomiting, diarrhea, agitation, combativeness) without added safety benefit, and can complicate the clinical encounter (a distressed, combative patient is harder to safely observe and treat).

Precautions: nalmefene's longer duration is a double-edged feature — it's the intended advantage against long-acting opioids, but it also means a precipitated withdrawal episode, if it occurs, lasts longer and is harder to manage than a naloxone-induced one.
pearls: The evidence-based default remains standard-dose naloxone (0.04-0.4 mg IV/IM, or the standard 4mg intranasal product), titrated to adequate ventilation, with re-dosing and a continuous infusion for recurrent re-sedation — see tox-opioids for that full approach. These high-dose/long-acting products are not shown to outperform that approach and add real over-reversal risk.

Reach for Kloxxado/Opvee only where your protocol or product availability specifically calls for it (e.g. a take-home naloxone program that has standardized on the higher-dose product, or an EMS system protocol built around it) rather than reflexively assuming 'higher dose = better' for a suspected fentanyl overdose.

Community/bystander naloxone distribution programs increasingly stock these higher-dose products for logistical/availability reasons as much as clinical superiority — worth knowing what a patient or their community contacts may already have access to and have used before ED arrival.
